item.title: The Future of Personal Coding Harnesses
item.description:
Why the next generation of coding agents will be shaped by their users, not their vendors.

Some time passed since my last post. As I was calling out on one of my previous posts last year, lots of adoption is currently happening across companies, which keeps me very busy with work helping them in their transformation process.

I still plan to post about my local setup and to revisit some points I made on my “Lessons from a Brownfield Project” post, but this will probably come towards the end of this year.

item.title: Security in the agentic era
item.description:
In my last post I mentioned that “security is not optional”, touching briefly on the lethal trifecta, data leakage and sandboxing. With this post I want to show some concrete examples of why security is extremely important, especially when rolling out agentic workflows in enterprises.

Security, as always, is for most people an afterthought. In the agentic era, it is actually very scary what you can achieve with minimal effort. This motivated me in recent months to show customers and our colleagues in trainings what attacks can look like. Their faces during the demo are always priceless. So, in the words of Steve Yegge, be scared!

item.title: My Debugging Workflow with Agents
item.description:
Debugging is where agents shine a lot. I briefly touched on this in my previous post and I think this topic deserves its own deep dive, because the workflow is more nuanced than just “paste the error and let the agent fix it”. Over months of real-world usage, I developed three levels of debugging that I apply based on how nasty the bug is.

Most bugs are simple. You paste the error, add some context, and the agent nails it. But some bugs fight back. For those, you need a system. Here are my three levels.

item.title: Six Months of Agentic Coding in the Trenches: Lessons from a Brownfield Project
item.description:
Let’s recap my journey of using various AI tools in a real customer project. The project was going for two years and focused primarily on modernization. What started as legacy hell, is now more maintainable. Deployments are more frequent and the customer gained more confidence developing new features.

The journey is split into three waves of AI usage and the last six months represent the last, third wave, which changed the way I work completely.
